'''Esther Szekeres''' ({{langx|hu|Klein Eszter}}; {{nee|'''Klein'''}}; 20 February 1910{{spaced ndash}}28 August 2005) was a Hungarian–Australian [[mathematician]].

==Early life and education==
Esther Klein was born to Ignaz Klein in a Jewish family in [[Budapest]], [[Kingdom of Hungary]], on 20 February 1910. As a young physics student in Budapest,<ref name="smh"/> Klein was a member of a group of Hungarians including [[Paul Erdős]], [[George Szekeres]], [[Pál Turán]],<ref name="St Andrews"/><ref>{{cite web | title=George Szekeres|first =J J|last= O'Connor |first2=E F|last2= Robertson|date =March 2006 | website=Maths History | publisher =Mactutor| url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Szekeres/ | access-date=8 March 2026}} Creative Commons Licence 4.0</ref> and her old schoolfriend [[Márta Svéd]] (then Wachsberger), who convened over interesting mathematical problems, often at the [[Anonymous (statue)|Anonymous]] in [[Budapest City Park]]. Klein was known as Epsz by Svéd.<ref name=universe>{{cite book| title=A Universe of Sufficient Size| first= Miriam|last= Sved| chapter=Acknowledgements| page= 312-313|ISBN= 9781743535127|date=2019 }}</ref> 

In 1933, Klein proposed to the group a [[combinatorics|combinatorial]] problem that Erdős named as the "[[Happy Ending problem]]", as it led to her marriage to George Szekeres.<ref name="smh"/> Erdős and George Szekeres went on to publish about the problem, but Esther was not mentioned as taking part later.<ref name=universe/>

==Career==
Following the outbreak of [[World War II]] in 1939, Esther and George Szekeres emigrated to Australia after spending the wartime years in [[Hongkou District|Hongkew]], a community of refugees located in [[Shanghai]], China,<ref name="hongkew"/> before moving to Australia in 1945. They first lived in [[Adelaide]], [[South Australia]], for three years<ref name="smh"/> where they shared a small apartment with Márta and her husband [[George Svéd]], with all of their children, before moving to [[Sydney]]<ref name=universe/> in 1964.

In Sydney, Esther lectured at [[Macquarie University]] and was actively involved in mathematics enrichment for high-school students. In 1984, she jointly founded a weekly mathematics enrichment meeting that has since expanded into a programme of about 30 groups that continue to meet weekly and inspire high school students throughout Australia and New Zealand.<ref name="amt"/>

==Personal life and death==
Esther married George Szekeres in 1937, and they had two children.<ref name="smh"/>

When they first moved to Australia after the war, the Szekeres shared an apartment in Adelaide with mathematician [[Márta Svéd]], an old school friend of Szekeres, and her husband [[George Svéd]], for three years,<ref name="smh"/> with their children.<ref name=universe/>

In 2004, she and George moved back to Adelaide, where, on 28 August 2005, she and her husband died within an hour of each other.<ref name="St Andrews"/><ref name="smh"/><ref name=universe/> Esther's friend Márta Svéd died a month later, also in Adelaide.<ref name=universe/>

===In fiction===
The Svéds' granddaughter, author [[Miriam Sved]],<ref>{{cite web| url=https://historicalnovelsociety.org/reviews/a-universe-of-sufficient-size/| website= Historical Novel Society| title=A Universe of Sufficient Size, Written by Miriam Sved| first =Georgia Rose| last= Phillips|quote= Appeared in: ''HNR'' Issue 90 (November 2019) | date= November 2019| access-date=9 March 2026}}</ref><ref name=hardy>{{cite web | last=Hardy | first=Karen | title=Miriam Sved: Game Day novel on the ball | website=The Sydney Morning Herald | date=14 August 2014 | url=https://www.smh.com.au/entertainment/books/miriam-sved-game-day-novel-on-the-ball-20140814-103x8y.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240804212857/https://www.smh.com.au/entertainment/books/miriam-sved-game-day-novel-on-the-ball-20140814-103x8y.html | archive-date=4 August 2024 | url-status=live | access-date=9 March 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last=Sved | first=Miriam | title=fiction | website=[[Overland (magazine)]] | date=15 April 2013 | url=https://overland.org.au/previous-issues/issue-198/fiction-miriam-sved/ | access-date=9 March 2026}}</ref> wrote the historical novel ''A Universe of Sufficient Size'', published in 2019.<ref>{{cite web | title= Miriam Sved | website=Miriam Sved – Author | url=https://miriamsved.com.au/about/ | access-date=9 March 2026}}</ref> It tells the story of a group of Jewish mathematicians in Hungary who flee the country, which she based on stories she had heard from Márta Svéd. While the story is fictional, several characters are loosely based on people in Svéd's circle, in particular Esther and George Szekeres, as well as Paul Erdős.<ref name=universe/>

==Recognition==
In 1990, Macquarie gave Szekeres an [[honorary doctorate]].<ref name="smh"/>

In 1993, she was the recipient of a [[BH Neumann Award]] of the Australian Mathematics Trust.<ref name="neumann"/>
